rows.label: Formula
rows.text:
Absolute error Δx
Relative error = Δx / x
Percentage error = (Δx / x) × 100%

rows.label: Conditions
rows.text: Averaging does not remove a systematic zero error.  ·  Relative errors add for a product. Absolute errors do not simply add as the final answer without that rule.

rows.label: Special cases
rows.text: Least count is the smallest division and sets a lower bound on the absolute error of one reading.  ·  A gross mistake is discarded, not averaged in.

rows.label: Solved
rows.text: An error is the difference between a measured value and the true value. A systematic error repeats in the same direction, as when a metre scale has a worn zero end. A random error scatters readings both ways and is reduced by averaging.  ·  The best estimate from n readings is their arithmetic mean. The absolute error of one reading is its difference from the mean. The mean absolute error is the average of those differences, taken as positive.

rows.label: Limitation
rows.text: The order of magnitude is a power of ten, not the significant-figure count.  ·  A percentage error is not the absolute error. It is the absolute error as a percent of the value.

rows.label: Study notes
rows.text: The result is written as mean ± mean absolute error. The relative error is that absolute error divided by the mean. The percentage error is the relative error times 100.  ·  When quantities are multiplied or divided, relative errors add. If z = xy, then Δz/z = Δx/x + Δy/y, using the absolute values of the relative errors. For a power, z = x^n, the relative error is multiplied by n.  ·  Scientific notation writes a number as a coefficient between 1 and 10 times a power of ten. The order of magnitude is that power of ten after the coefficient is used to decide the nearest power. A coefficient of 3 or more often rounds the order upward in the rough classroom rule of 'greater than about sqrt(10)' .
